Good morning. I call to order the high-level meeting on the theme Preventing and Combating Illicit Trafficking in Wildlife and Other Crimes That Affect the Environment. As mentioned in my letters dated May 8th and June 1st, 2026, this high-level debate is held pursuant to Resolution 80/229 of December 18th, 2025,— and aims to raise awareness on the scale and complexity of crimes that affect the environment and their impact on security, sustainable development and human rights. This meeting will offer a platform to reiterate the strategic importance of preventing and combating this type of crime, to share information on their trends and exchange good practice in responding to them. This meeting will also contribute to addressing the relationship between crimes that affect the environment and corruption. A summary of today's discussion will be transmitted at the Commission on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice and to all member states. I will now deliver my statement as President of the General Assembly. Excellencies, thank you for joining this morning's high-level debate on preventing and combating illicit trafficking in wildlife and other crimes that affect the environment. This important topic touches upon a wide range of interconnected concerns: biodiversity, law and order, peace and security, health and well-being, sustainable development, and economic growth. Mirroring the interdependency of the three pillars of our Charter. Its comprehensive nature is a reminder that these crimes not only jeopardize our environment but pose threats to our societies, institutions, and economies. Consider a few recent examples. In Kenya, authorities apprehended smugglers attempting to sell thousands of Queen African harvester ants, primarily in Europe and Asia. Here in the United States, an individual has been charged with poaching nearly 2,000 turtles from Florida for illegal sale in Taiwan. And in the Democratic Republic of Congo, recent mudslides triggered the collapse of unapproved and unregulated mines where criminal networks were allegedly extracting critical minerals and precious metals. Hundreds reportedly perished. And these are only examples from the last few months. UNODC's World Life Crime Report shows that wildlife crime remains a persistent global threat involving more than 160 countries and targeting thousands of species worldwide. Illegal deforestation, perhaps the most visible and well-documented of these crimes, accounts for over 40% of deforestation in tropical forests. All told, these crimes funnel resources to organized criminal networks, undermine the rule of law, enable tax evasion, and fuel corruption, all the while reducing financing for sustainable development. They also contribute to diversity loss, disrupt ecosystems, dismantle carbon sinks, and jeopardize human health and well-being. The evidence of this is clear. Removing queen ants from Kenya, for instance, could lead to the collapse of thousands of colonies and the loss of billions of ants disrupting ecosystems and affecting pollination and agriculture. And illicit trade in critical minerals and precious resources costs countries like the DRC billions of dollars in revenue annually, with much of it landing in the hands of criminal networks and rebel groups, jeopardizing peace and security. Today's debate is thus an opportunity to help address these interconnected challenges, raise awareness, strengthen implementation, and to make better use of the tools already at our disposal. This includes multilateral frameworks such as the United Nations Convention Against Transnational Organized Crime and the United Nations Convention Against Corruption. It includes environmental agreements such as the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora and the Basel Convention on the Control of boundary movements of hazards, waste, and their disposal. And it includes programs that are already delivering results, such as UNODC's Global Programme on Crimes that Affect the Environment, which supports national and regional authorities through strengthened legislation, enhanced law enforcement cooperation, and efforts to disrupt illicit financial flows and organized criminal activity. Excellencies, the forthcoming 13th session of the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Convention Against Transnational Organized Crimes to be held this October offers an important opportunity to advance a more coordinated and harmonized response to illicit trafficking in wildlife and other crimes that affect the environment. Because as today's discussion makes clear, these are not isolated crimes with isolated consequences. They are interconnected threats that demand interconnected solutions. So let us use today not simply to diagnose the problem, but to identify practical ways forward, to strengthen cooperation, make better use of existing mechanisms, and build the collective response this challenge demands, again in the spirit of knowing that we are always better together. By this, I give the floor to Miss Monica Juma, Executive Director of the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, and thank you for her work and congratulate her for taking up her new role.

Your Excellency, Ms. Annalena Baerbock, President of the General Assembly, distinguished speakers, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, I am honored to address this Assembly at its first-ever high-level debate dedicated to crimes that affect the environment. I would like to commend you, Madam President, for convening this timely and historic discussion. For too long, these crimes were viewed primarily through a conservation lens, but that framing is no longer sufficient because what is at stake is far more than the loss of biodiversity. It is the destruction of ecosystems, the loss of livelihoods, the harm done to communities, and the erosion of the rule of law. What we are confronting today is a rapidly evolving form of transnational organized crime that is exploiting natural resources, weakening institutions, and generating illicit profits on a global scale. Whether it is wildlife, timber, minerals, fisheries, or waste, These resources are being extracted, trafficked, and monetized through sophisticated criminal enterprises operating across sectors, across borders, across regions, globally. The matter at hand is about the ability of states to exercise authority over their territory, safeguard their natural wealth, support their economies, and protect the well-being of their citizens. Today's debate is therefore an important step in recognizing crimes that affect the environment not simply as environmental issues but as matters of justice, of security, and the rule of law, especially as these activities increasingly overlap with other forms of organized crime. The same networks involved in wildlife trafficking may also engage in in drug trafficking, arms trafficking, and human trafficking for forced labor. Different commodities, different markets, but the same criminal business model. As we see this model play out across all regions, in the Amazon Basin, organized criminal groups are destroying forests, polluting rivers, and challenging state authority through illegal logging and mining. In the Golden Triangle, crimes that affect the environment are intertwined with the illicit drug economy, creating criminal markets that reinforce one another. In the Sahel, gold and diamonds are currencies of power and violence, financing armed groups and undermining governance in fragile context. And in my home country, Kenya, the recent smuggling of 2,200 live arms shows that even the smallest of species can mean big business for organized crime. These threats represent the commodification of nature by organized crime. They generate billions of dollars in illicit profits each year, fueling corruption and money laundering while distorting trade and legitimate economies. That is why they require a strong, coordinated criminal justice and law enforcement response. Excellencies, the international community has made important progress in recognizing the seriousness of these crimes. The General Assembly has adopted a series of resolutions addressing the many forms that wildlife trafficking and other crimes that affect the environment can take. The United Nations Convention Against Transnational Organized Crime provides the world's largest framework for international cooperation, including through mutual legal assistance, joint investigations, and law enforcement cooperation. And in its provisions are highly relevant to addressing the increasingly organized and cross-border nature of crimes that affect the environment. The United Nations Convention Against Corruption, complements this framework by setting out measures to prevent and combat corruption as a key enabler of these types of crimes. And the recently adopted United Nations Convention Against Cybercrime gives us an important new tool to pursue these crimes in the digital sphere and facilitate the sharing of electronic evidence across jurisdictions. We have a robust international legal framework at our disposal. Yet this framework is only as strong as the justice systems that enforce it. This is where UNDOC's unique added value comes into play. Our mandate is clear and it is anchored in the resolutions agreed in this very hall. We support countries in strengthening criminal justice responses to crimes that affect the environment. We build the capacity of law enforcement agencies, prosecutors, judges, and frontline officers to investigate, to prosecute, and adjudicate these crimes more effectively. In doing so, we complement the work of the other UN entities engaged in environmental protection, including the United Nations Environment Programme, by bringing a unique rule of law component to this issue. We also generate evidence and data through our research products such as the Wildlife Crime Report and the Global Analysis on Crimes That Affect the Environment. And as the guardian and secretariat of the conventions, we assist member states with implementation, legislative guidance, and strengthening institutional frameworks. This work has in turn informed and shaped our, our operational impact. In 2025 alone, UNODC trained more than 3,000 officials. We supported more than 80 investigations, and we contributed to enforcement operations across 59 countries, which led to over 200 wildlife and timber seizures. These results demonstrate what is possible when political will, is matched by operational cooperation and sustained investment. Excellencies, while we have come a long way in recognizing this threat, there are still gaps that we must address. First, we must close legislative and enforcement loopholes. In many jurisdictions, crimes that affect the environment are still not treated with the seriousness they require. Too often, Penalties are insufficient to deter criminal conduct. Too often, these crimes are detected but not adequately investigated and prosecuted. And too often, they fall below the threshold of serious crime under the Convention Against Transnational Crime— organized crime, limiting opportunities for international cooperation and the deployment of specialized investigative techniques. For example, while 86% of member states have criminalized offenses against wildlife, fewer than half have imposed penalties of at least 4 years imprisonment for these offenses. In other words, the legislative architecture is largely in place, but it is unevenly applied. And this is precisely— and it is precisely these gaps and vulnerabilities that criminal networks exploit and which we must strive to close. Second, we must widen the evidence base. We know a great deal about certain forms of these crimes, but significant blind spots remain, particularly in the area of illegal mining, illegal fishing, and waste crime. Better data means better policy, and better policy means effective enforcement. Third, we must engage the private sector as a strategic partner. Criminal markets increasingly intersect with legitimate economies and global supply chains. Businesses have an important role to play in strengthening due diligence, identifying suspicious activity, bringing innovative technology to the table, and preventing illicit commodities from entering legal markets. And fourth, we must follow the money. Every shipment of illegally harvested timber, every trafficked wildlife product, every illicit mineral transaction generates a financial trail that can expose criminal networks, corrupt facilitators, and the beneficiaries behind these crimes. Financial investigations must therefore become a routine component of enforcement. By targeting criminal profits and disrupting illicit financial flows, we can put an end to the business model that sustains these activities. Ladies and gentlemen, this debate sends an important signal on several fronts. It signals our collective responsibility to prevent and stop the exploitation of nature for profit. And it signals that the international community is ready to treat these crimes as part of the broader security, justice, and the rule of law agenda. I hope that this leads to a stronger, more coordinated global response as we work together to protect our planet and its precious natural treasures for the benefit of humanity today and the future generations to come. I thank you for your kind attention.

I thank the Executive Director of the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime. I give the floor to His Excellency Rüdiger Bohn, Chair of the Commission on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice and the Permanent Representative of Germany to the United Nations in Vienna.

Madam President, Mrs. Juma, distinguished delegates, it is an honor to address this high-level debate on preventing and combating illicit trafficking in wildlife and other crimes that affect the environment. I commend the President of the General Assembly for convening for this timely discussion and for bringing us together around an issue of growing global concern. Crimes that affect the environment pose a serious and evolving threat to sustainable development, the rule of law, and international security. They undermine governance, fuel corruption, and generate illicit financial flows. Addressing these crimes requires coordinated, evidence-based, and sustained action across jurisdictions. The Commission on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice, as the United Nations' principal policymaking body in crime prevention and criminal justice, plays a central role in advancing international responses. It also serves as the governing body for the crime-related work of the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, including its efforts to prevent and counter crimes that affect the environment which will be presented in greater detail by Mrs. Juma and UNODC colleagues later today in a side event. So what has been accomplished so far? First, the Commission has provided a strong normative foundation. It began addressing environmental protection as early as 1994 through a resolution on the role of criminal law. Since then, it has negotiated numerous resolutions on specific norms for illicit trafficking. Particularly in protected species of wild fauna and flora, as well as timber and forest products. The broader concept of crimes that affect the environment was first used in a resolution negotiated in 2021, subsequently endorsed by the General Assembly. Most recently, in 2025, the Commission negotiated a comprehensive resolution later adopted by the General Assembly on tackling illicit trafficking in world fauna and flora, including timber and timber products, the illegal mining of and illicit trafficking in minerals and precious metals, illicit trafficking in waste, and other crimes that affect the environment. This resolution reflects a growing consensus that these crimes are closely linked to corruption, money laundering, and organized crime and must be addressed through coordinated and multidisciplinary responses. Second, the Commission has facilitated important policy dialogues. In February 2022, it convened expert discussions with over 800 participants from 94 countries. These discussions highlighted key priorities. On prevention, experts emphasized the need to address root causes, reduce demand, raise awareness, strengthen supply chain integrity, and address links with other crimes and improve data collection. On enforcement, they stressed the need for comprehensive criminal justice responses from crime scene to court, ensuring that detection leads to investigation, prosecution, and adjudication. They also highlighted the importance of following the money, confiscating criminal proceeds, and holding perpetrators accountable. Particular attention was given to ensuring access to justice, public participation, and the protection of affected communities, including indigenous peoples and local communities. Experts further underlined the importance of strengthening international cooperation, both through enhanced interagency coordination among coordination organizations such as CITES, Interpol, UNODC, the World Bank, and the World Customs Organization, and through increased technical assistance and capacity building. Thematic discussions held in 2024 and 2025 reaffirmed the need for deeper international collaboration. A persistent challenge remains the absence of a commonly accepted definition of crimes that affect the environment, which affects legal clarity and complicates data collection as well as international cooperation. Third, the United Nations Congresses on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice —the largest global forum for criminal justice policy, which is prepared by the Commission every 5 years—have provided the policy framework for the Commission's action. Since 1990, these congresses have emphasized the role of criminal law and environmental protection. Most recently, the 14th Crime Congress held in Kyoto in 2021 reaffirmed the need for effective measures to prevent and combat such crimes by making the best possible use of relevant international instruments and through stronger legislation enhanced international cooperation, capacity building, and improved law enforcement. Fourth, other intergovernmental processes serviced by UNODC have also advanced this agenda. The Conferences of the Parties of the United Nations Convention Against Transnational Organized Crime, UNTOC COP, and the United Nations Convention Against Corruption, UNCAC COP, COSP, both addresses crimes affecting the environment. The Commission has consistently encouraged the recognition of these crimes as serious crimes as defined under the Organized Crime Convention, thereby enabling stronger international cooperation mechanisms. The Assembly welcomed in 2025 in its Resolution 80/227, which had been negotiated within the Commission in Vienna, the establishment of of the Open-Ended Intergovernmental Expert Group under the Organized Crime Convention. Its mandate is to assess implementation, identify gaps in the international legal framework, and consider possible responses, including the feasibility of an additional protocol to the convention. The group has met twice and will report its findings in October this year. So what lies ahead? Looking forward, the 15th United Nations Crime Congress, to be held in Abu Dhabi from 26th of September to the 1st of October 2026 will provide a critical opportunity to advance this agenda. Its overarching theme on accelerating crime prevention, criminal justice, and the rule of law to protect people and planet and achieve the 2030 Agenda underscores the importance of addressing environmental crime. Crimes that affect the environment are currently being discussed in the negotiations on the Abu Dhabi Declaration, which is expected to be adopted on the opening day of the forthcoming Congress and to guide international action for the next 5 years. The negotiations reflect both progress and ongoing challenges, including differing views on definitions, legislative gaps, and the potential development of an additional protocol. The Crime Congress will also provide member states with an opportunity to make concrete implementation-focused commitments under the Pledge for Justice initiative. The issue will moreover feature prominently in high-level meetings, workshops, particularly the one on data collection and analysis, and a wide range of side events and exhibitions. Madam President, distinguished delegates, crimes that affect the environment are not isolated phenomena. They are transnational and deeply embedded in broader patterns of organized crime and corruption. Addressing them requires sustained political will, robust legal frameworks, effective enforcement, and strong international cooperation. The Commission remains committed to supporting member states in these efforts through policy development, knowledge sharing, and fostering partnerships across sectors and regions. Let us continue to work together to protect our environment, uphold the rule of law, and ensure a sustainable future for generations to come. I thank you.
I thank the Chair of the Commission on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice. I give the floor to Ms. Greta Aguilar, Director-General of the International Union for Conservation of Nature.

Madam President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen. It is an honor to address this high-level debate on behalf of the International Union for Conservation of Nature, IUCN, in existence for 78 years and now the world's largest global environmental network composed of state members and civil society. Excellencies, today the international community comes together to confront one of the most urgent and often underrecognized challenges of our time: preventing and combating crimes that affect the environment. Decisive action on this will determine the quality of our future. As we humans depend on a healthy environment to thrive. Crimes that affect the environment are one of the largest and fastest growing criminal activities worldwide. They include wildlife trafficking, illegal logging and deforestation, illegal mining, the illegal activities of unselective illegal fishing, pollution crimes, and other self-environmental destruction, including destruction linked to armed conflict. These are complex transactional and organized criminal activities that destroy biodiversity, destabilize ecosystems, and erode livelihoods, and pose a direct threat to human security. Increasingly, the same network involved in environmental crime are also trafficking drugs, weapons, and human beings. These are intentional crimes that generate billions of dollars. Crimes that affect the environment are accelerating biodiversity loss at an alarming pace. Iconic species such as elephants, rhinos, tigers, sea turtles, jaguars, and pangolins have become tragic symbols of this crisis. But the impact extends far beyond them. Entire ecosystems are degraded as illegal logging clears forests, unselective and unmonitored fishing depletes oceans, and illegal mining and pollution poisons soils and waterways, harming both nature and communities worldwide. Environmental destruction is further intensified by armed conflict through damage to ecosystems, the exploitation of natural resources, and the breakdown of environmental governance. And in turn, as resources are depleted, further tensions raise and conflicts emerge or intensify, creating a vicious circle we must break. Indigenous peoples and local communities, among the most effective stewards of biodiversity, often face displacement, loss of livelihoods, and risk when defending their lands and resources. This is happening, Excellencies, every day while they defend their communities, and their resources. Environmental defenders are increasingly threatened and in some cases face violence and even loss of life. This is unacceptable. Individuals and communities that protect nature must never have to do so at the risk of their own life. Excellencies, as we work to prevent and combat crimes that affect the environment, we must recognize the profound human dimension. Environmental crime is not only an ecological crisis, it is a fundamental threat to development, governance, and human security. As highlighted by the UN Rapporteur on Human Rights and the Environment, illegal activities affecting the environment and environmental degradation are increasingly intertwined with serious human rights violations, including impacts on the right to life, health, food, and healthy environment. Yet despite the scale of this threat, a critical gap remains. At the UN level, there is no dedicated international legal framework to prevent and combat the crimes that affect the environment. No country can tackle this challenge alone. A stronger multilateral and multisector cooperation is essential. A notable development is the adoption of the Council of Europe Convention on the Protection of the Environment through Criminal Law in May 2025. This is the first international legally binding instrument to address crimes that affect the environment. Combating a broad range of criminal acts that aggravate the triple planetary crisis of climate change, pollution, and biodiversity loss. The convention opened for signature last December, and we are hopeful that it soon will enter into force. We in IUCN remain committed to advancing global action through science, policy, and collaboration. Our strategic vision to 2045 reaffirms our commitment to environmental justice, the protection of people, and action against environmental crime. The upcoming UN Crime Congress in Abu Dhabi provides a timely and important opportunity to further strengthen international cooperation on these issues. Excellencies, if we are to safeguard biodiversity, and uphold human security and human rights, we must act decisively and collectively. We must treat environmental crime as a serious global threat, empower indigenous peoples and local communities, protect environmental defenders, strengthen regional, international, and multi-sector cooperation, because only together we can stop nature crimes, strengthen the capacity of member states to prevent and prosecute crimes that affect the environment, and lastly, we must close legal and governance gaps at national and international levels. The cost of inaction is too high, Excellencies. Every forest illegally cleared, Every species trafficked, every ecosystem degraded bring us closer to irreversible loss. The clock is ticking and we cannot lose time. By working together, we can stop the crimes that affect the environment. What we need now is a stronger political will, shared responsibility, and collective action. Let us raise this challenge together because protecting nature is not only about conserving biodiversity. It is about securing a safe and sustainable future for our planet and for our people. I thank you for your attention.

I thank the Director-General of the International Union for Conservation of nature. We've heard the last speaker for the opening segment. As indicated in the program, this high-level debate consists of a plenary segment for interventions from member states and observers of the Assembly. The plenary segment will begin immediately following the conclusion of this opening segment and will continue until 1 PM and then from 3 to 6 PM in this hall. We will now begin the plenary segment. To allow maximum participation by all, members are requested to limit their interventions to 5 minutes when speaking on behalf of a group— sorry, when speaking on behalf of member states. Sorry again. Request to limit their intervention to 5 minutes when speaking on behalf of a group and 3 minutes when speaking in national capacity. Time limits will be strictly enforced through an automatic microphone cutoff. To assist speakers with time management, a timer will be projected on the screens. I thank you for your cooperation. As the first speaker, I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Brazil, also speaking on behalf of the Coalition for Multilateral Action Against Crimes that Crimes That Affect the Environment, speaking time of 5 minutes, followed by the European Union and Malawi.

Madam President, I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the 23 members of the Coalition for Multilateral Action Against Crimes That Affect the Environment, supported by 13 civil society organizations from different regions. The full version of the text will be available in the UN Journal. Launched in Rio de Janeiro in November 2025, the Coalition works to promote multilateral action against crimes that affect the environment and the establishment of a binding legal framework under the UN Convention Against Transnational Organized Crime, the TOC, to tackle this challenge. I thank you for organizing this timely debate promoting synergies among this General Assembly and other multilateral discussions on crimes that affect the environment. These crimes pose multiple challenges to the international community, including their significant negative impacts on biodiversity and sustainable development. They destabilize societies and economies, indigenous peoples and local communities, sustain organized criminal networks engaged in broader illicit illicit activities deprive governments of revenue and local communities of income. The growing involvement of organized criminal networks and the interconnection of crimes that affect the environment and other forms of transnational organized crime, including money laundering, corruption, illicit financial flows, trafficking, firearms, and drug trafficking, is a matter of particular concern. According to the Financial Action Task Force, these crimes generate up to $281 billion annually, placing them among the most profitable forms of transnational crime, while the World Bank estimates the value of the impacts of a subset of crimes that affect the environment in the trillions of dollars. Madam President, while recognition of The threat posed by crimes that affect the environment has been growing in the most affected parts of the world. A comprehensive response from the international community is still lacking. Domestic and regional efforts are required but not sufficient to face such a growing transnational challenge, which depends on effective and reliable international cooperation. The existing gaps in the The international legal framework seriously constrained the fight against crimes that affect the environment. Establishing a binding legal framework under the UN Convention Against Transnational Organized Crime to counter crimes that affect the environment is an urgent necessity. It would provide a basis to strengthen international legal and police cooperation to support support the international community in fulfilling its shared responsibility to prevent and combat such crimes. The next Conference of Parties in October will be a decisive moment in this process. Madam President, I will now make a few additional remarks in my national capacity. Brasil understands that the UN has a central role to play by establishing an additional protocol to the Palermo Convention dedicated to countering the most relevant forms of environmental crimes that fall within its scope: illicit traffic in wildlife, illegal mining, and illicit trafficking in waste. The upcoming UNTOC conference makes 2026 a pivotal moment for the international community to take action against these crimes. Together with the coalition, Brazil will work towards the adoption at the upcoming COP of a resolution that launches negotiations on the Additional Protocol. There is also good reason to believe that the number of members of the coalition will grow meaningfully in the upcoming weeks. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Brazil. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the European Union on behalf of the EU and its member states.

Thank you, President. I have the honor to speak on behalf of the European Union and its member states. The candidate countries North Macedonia, Montenegro, Albania, Ukraine, the Republic of Moldova, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Georgia, as well as Armenia, Andorra, and San Marino, align themselves with this statement. We welcome this timely high-level debate. Environmental crimes, particularly the illicit trafficking in wildlife, have evolved into a highly sophisticated industrial-scale form of transnational organized crime. They generate billions in criminal wealth, strip local populations of natural resources and their livelihoods, and directly accelerate the triple planetary crisis of pollution, climate change, and biodiversity loss. Environmental crime is a global threat affecting all regions, but it is particularly devastating to to the critical ecosystems of the three basins: the Amazon, Congo, and Mekong. We are conscious of Europe's role as a transit point for various trafficking routes worldwide, as well as a destination region for pet trade markets. And we recognize the responsibility that this entails, as highlighted by Europol's Serious and Organized Crime Threat Assessment. Associated challenges include not only wildlife trafficking but a broader spectrum of crimes that affect the environment, including acts causing environmental degradation, illicit waste dumping, and natural resource depletion. These offenses are no longer isolated conservation issues. They're often deeply interlinked with drug trafficking, systemic systemic corruption and other forms of organized crime. This reality requires closer coordination between law enforcement authorities, border management services, customs, environmental agencies, and the judiciary to ensure coherent detection, investigation, and prosecution of those responsible. Crimes that affect on the environment heavily impact Indigenous peoples and local communities due to their close connection to nature. They, together with rangers and nature defenders, are on the front line of protection, facing severe threats. It is crucial that attacks against environmental and land defenders are thoroughly investigated and prosecuted, and that national authorities have the capacity and tools to protect those at risk. To turn multilateral policy into genuine impact, we recall recent consensus. The EU and its member states welcome last year's resolution on the topic tabled by Brazil at the Commission on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice. We also express our sincere appreciation to Peru in its capacity as chair of the United Nations Convention Against Transnational Organized Crime expert group on crimes that affect the environment, and look forward to engaging with all delegations, international organizations, and civil society in the run-up to the 13th Conference of Parties to the Palermo Convention. However, major challenges remain, including fragmented legal frameworks, corruption, and the rapid shift of illegal trade to digital spaces. The existing international legal framework, anchored by the Convention on international trade in endangered species of wild fauna and flora, UNCAC and UNTAC, is vital, but it contains blind spots that criminal networks exploit. To strengthen this, we must address the convergence between environmental crime, corruption, and illicit financial flows. The current discussions regarding a possible additional protocol to the UNTAC on crimes that affect the environment providing opportunity to look at coordination and legal alignment issues. UN resources are under pressure, and we must encourage agencies to work together through flexible multi-stakeholder models. We must deepen public-private partnerships with technology, e-commerce, and shipping sectors to clean up supply chains. Existing EU and international law enforcement cooperation frameworks, including those supported by Europol and Interpol, must be further leveraged to systematically target the criminal networks behind environmental crimes. President, the EU and its member states remain firmly confirmed to strengthening the fight against crimes that affect the environment. We call upon all global partners to reinforce international cooperation, enhance enforcement capacities, and protect both our global ecosystems and the rule of law.

I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the European Union. I now have the— give the floor to the distinguished representative of Malawi on behalf of the Africa Group.

Mr. President, distinguished delegates, I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the African Group. The African Group thanks you for convening this important debate on preventing and combating illicit trafficking in wildlife and other crimes that affect the environment. For Africa, this issue goes far beyond conservation. It is fundamentally about sustainable development, economic resilience, good governance, and the sustainable management of natural resources. Environmental crimes continue to undermine biodiversity, weaken livelihoods, fuel corruption and organized crime, and contribute to illicit financial flows that drain much-needed resources from our economies. For millions of Africans, nature is not an abstract concept. It is a source of food, income, environment, employment, and opportunity. Protecting biodiversity, therefore, means protecting people, communities, and the foundations of sustainable development. Mr. President, Africa has consistently demonstrated its commitment to addressing these challenges through the African Union Strategy on Combating Illegal Exploitation and Illegal Trade in Wild Fauna and Flora, As well as those through national, regional, and cross-border initiatives, African countries have strengthened cooperation, enhanced law enforcement efforts, and promoted more sustainable management of natural resources. We also reaffirm the principle of the permanent sovereignty of states over their natural resources and the right of every country to manage those resources in accordance with its national priorities and development aspirations. As an African proverb reminds us, a tree does not stand alone in the forest. While African countries remain fully committed to addressing these challenges, last Finding solutions will require stronger international cooperation and shared responsibility. Combating environmental crimes requires stronger cooperation among countries of origin, transit, and destination. It also requires greater efforts to reduce demand, dismantle criminal networks, and tackle the illicit financial flows that enable these activities to flourish. In this regard, support for developing countries remains critical. Strengthened national capacities, technological transfer, technical assistance, and predictable financing are essential to enable effective conservation efforts and sustainable natural resource management. Africa continues to lose valuable resources through the illegal exploitation and trafficking of natural assets. Addressing these losses is not only an environmental imperative, it is also essential for domestic resource mobilization, economic transformation, and sustainable development. Mr. President, The African Group firmly believes that environmental protection and development must advance hand in hand. Africa's natural resources should not be viewed solely as assets to be protected. They are also strategic assets for economic transformation, job creation, poverty eradication, and the achievement of their aspirations contained in Agenda 2063 and Agenda 2030. At the same time, conservation cannot succeed without people. Local communities must be partners and beneficiaries in the protection and sustainable use of natural resources. When communities see tangible benefits, conservation becomes more effective and more inclusive and more sustainable. Natural resources of Africa constitute one of the continent's greatest assets. Their illegal exploitation is not merely a loss for the countries concerned, it is a loss for sustainable development and for future generations. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Malawi. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Ecuador.

Mr. President, environmental crimes are among the most lucrative and sophisticated manifestations of transnational organized crime. These illicit activities worsen ecosystems, degrade them, undermine economies, deepen social inequalities, and are carried out by transnational criminal networks linked to corruption, money laundering, and other illicit activities. For Ecuador, an extremely diverse country that serves as a custodian of ecosystems of global importance, these criminal activities constitute a direct threat to its biodiversity and natural heritage. This scourge endangers emblematic species and fragile ecosystems such as the Galápagos Islands, and the Amazon. In addressing this challenge, Ecuador would highlight the importance of the full implementation of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora, CITES, which must go hand in hand with strengthening national capacities to combat the illegal trade in protected species. Illegal mining is another particularly serious threat to countries in the Amazon region. Its effects go far beyond the illicit extraction of minerals. It destroys forests and water sources, accelerates deforestation, and severely affects biodiversity. Mr. President, the transnational and multifaceted nature of environmental crimes requires instruments that are capable of confronting the criminal networks that exploit regulatory and jurisdictional gaps. The development of a binding framework under the United Nations Convention Against Transnational Organized Crime would help to strengthen and improve international legal and law enforcement cooperation and promote more effective collaboration among judicial, customs, environmental, and financial authorities, particularly with regard to information sharing and financial traceability. The protection of the environment cannot be separated from the protection of our societies and of our common future. Combating illicit wildlife trafficking and illegal mining requires political will, effective international cooperation, and a firm commitment to multilateralism. And finally, my delegation endorses— aligns itself with the statement delivered by the permanent representative of Brazil on behalf of the Coalition for Multilateral Action Against Crimes That Affect the Environment. Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Ecuador. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Israel.

Thank you, Mr. President. For Israel, preventing and combating wildlife trafficking and other crimes that affect the environment are not only abstract challenges. In recent months, Israel Police and Israel Nature Parks Authority have encountered cases involving the illegal trade in lion cubs, primates, elephants and other protected species. The risks extended beyond the harm to animals themselves. Illegal trade can lead to the spread of invasive species, destabilize ecosystems, and increase zoonotic disease risks. Therefore, wildlife trafficking must be treated for what it is, serious transnational organized crime. The illegal trade in protected species and natural assets constitutes a major illicit economy generating substantial criminal revenues annually. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Indonesia.

Mr.

President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates. As one of the world's megadiverse archipelagic states, Indonesia shares the view that wildlife trafficking and other crimes that affect the environment are serious crimes threatening biodiversity, sustainable development, the rule of law, and livelihood of local communities. For Indonesia, this is no longer merely a conservation issue. Our vast territory and long coastlines create multiple entry points that are prone to trafficking routes. On this note, allow me to underline the importance of 3 points. First, stronger national deterrence. Through Law No. 32 of 2024, Indonesia has modernized its legal framework, including by strengthening penalties, establishing corporate liability, and extending protection to marine ecosystems. We have also intensified cyber patrols to detect, prosecute, and dismantle trafficking networks. Second, effective implementation of international legal frameworks. Indonesia supports stronger implementation of, among others, CITES, CBD, UNTOC, and relevant UN resolutions while respecting state sovereignty over natural resources. Stronger measures must be science-based, fair, and non-discriminatory. Moreover, standards on timber, wildlife, and biodiversity products should not become disguised barriers of trade, particularly when sustainable, legal, and community-based use supports poverty eradication and the livelihoods of local communities. Third, means of implementation and meaningful partnerships. International cooperation must be more practical and better resourced, including on capacity building, technology transfer, ensure digital monitoring, forensic tools and financial investigations, prosecution support, and wildlife rehabilitation. Indonesia continues to advance innovative financing for biodiversity. In 2025, we launched the Indonesia Biodiversity Fund to support key species protection, habitat restoration, local community capacity building, and biodiversity monitoring. This fund is an addition to our existing instruments such as SDG bond, green and blue bonds, and a coral reef bond. Thank you, Mr. President. Environmental crime Is now one of the fastest growing forms of organized crime. It drives nature loss, exacerbates poverty, fuels corruption and instability. It degrades the ecosystems on which food, water, health, supply chains and economies depend. The United Kingdom recognizes nature as a foundation of security and resilience, and environmental crime as a a direct threat to national security, growth, and climate. We remain committed to tackling illicit wildlife trafficking and other crimes, environmental crimes, building on a long history of delivering practical action. Through programs such as the Illegal Wildlife Trade Challenge Fund, we have supported 187 projects in 69 countries since 2014 to a total value of over £68 million. The Fund has pioneered approaches in financial crime, gender inclusion, law enforcement, and grassroots capacity building, delivering real-world outcomes and forging strong intersectoral partnerships. This experience also demonstrates the importance of locally led approaches. We recognize that communities and frontline defenders are often the most affected by environmental crime and they play a central role in delivering lasting change. To conclude, the transnational nature and scale of crime— crimes that affect the environment require a collective international response. We welcome the growing multilateral momentum to address environmental crime and embed it firmly within the international crime prevention agenda. This momentum was evident at the 35th session of the Commission on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice in Vienna last week, which provided a timely opportunity for crucial international engagement on shared challenges is opportunities for collective action. The United Kingdom stands ready to work with all countries and partners to deliver a more coordinated, ambitious, and effective international response. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the United Kingdom. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Angola.

Mr. President, Angola aligns itself with the statement delivered by Malawi on behalf of the African Group, and I will make additional remarks in my national capacity. We welcome the convening of this important debate on preventing and combating illicit trafficking in wildlife and other crimes that affect the environment. The protection of biodiversity and the sustainable development of natural resources remain key priorities for Angola. These are essential not only for environmental protection but also for sustainable development and well-being of our people. Environmental crimes continue to threaten ecosystems, undermine livelihoods, and deprive developing countries of resources needed for their economic and social progress. In response, Angola continues to stress its policies on biodiversity conservation, sustainable natural resource management, and environmental protection, in line with the UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the African Union Agenda 2063, and our National Development Plan 2023-27. We are also investing in the restoration of conservation areas and participating in regional and cross-border initiatives that promote biodiversity protection and support local community development. Mr. President, Angola recognizes that no country can address these challenges alone. Preventing and combating environmental crimes requires stronger international and regional cooperation, enhanced national capacities, greater access to technology, and adequate resources to support developing countries in their conservation efforts. In this regard, Angola reaffirms its support for the African Strategy on Combating Illegal Exploitation and Illegal Trade in Wild Fauna and Flora in Africa. We call for strengthened cooperation, intelligence sharing, capacity building, effective law enforcement, and community engagement as essential elements in combating wildlife trafficking and other environmental crimes. We also underscored the importance of addressing both the supply and demand dimensions of illicit wildlife trade, while ensuring that local communities benefit from conservation efforts and the sustainable use of natural resources. For Angola, protecting nature means safeguarding livelihoods, creating opportunities, and investing in more sustainable management for the present and future generations. I thank you.
